ten years of additional life expectancy. Singapore 
spends about 4 percent less of its income on health 
than others at the same level of development but 
achieves the same life expectancy. Other coun­
tries, of which Costa Rica and India are examples, 
obtain relatively good health results but also spend 
relatively more. (In the case of India health spend­
ing is low and health status is poor, but even lower 
spending and worse status would be expected for 
a country with such low levels of income and 
schooling.) Egypt and Zambia, by contrast, get 
poor health for a lower-than-predicted level of 
spending. Finally, it is possible both to spend more 
than predicted on health care and still achieve un­
expectedly poor results. The United States is an 
extreme case, spending 5 percent more of GNP 
54 
than predicted to achieve several years less of life 
expectancy than would be typical for its high in­
come and high educational level. 
Analyses using other measures of health status, 
such as child mortality, yield similar results. This 
raises obvious and important questions. What ac­
counts for these large deviations? How much is 
attributable to the characteristics of health sys­
tems? How can public policy help to provide better 
health outcomes for a given national effort?
